breastfeeding_challenge_impact_MH_descri: Yes. Breastfeeding was excruciating as my baby was tongue tied. Various medical professionals told me my baby was fine and the pain of breastfeeding was all in my head. However, my baby was so obviously tongue tied that even my husband and I could see it. We were told by midwives not to go for a private diagnosis as unscrupulous doctors who were 'in it for the money' would cut my daughter's tongue unnecessarily and may damage her ability to talk. Some midwives also said I was 'jumping on the bandwagon' and trying to follow 'a trend' and 'just because you've heard of a baby with tongue tie, you want yours to have it'. Over and over I was told by the midwives and breastfeeding support team from the hospital that I was doing it wrong, holding my baby in the wrong position and that was why it wasn't working. My nipples were so damaged that chunks of skin were falling off, and they were bleeding, but the breastfeeding expert at the hospital said she couldn't understand what my problem was and my baby was feeding fine. She watched my baby feed with milk leaking out of the corners of her mouth and said it was 'the best latch she'd ever seen'. Luckily, a breastfeeding support worker from Bambis agreed she may be tongue tied and referred us to an NHS service, but I waited months. By the time the tongue tie was diagnosed and treated, many months later, I was a nervous wreck due to the pain and not being believed. I had been given advice many times about how not breastfeeding exclusively was a risk factor in cot death. Bambis had also given me horrific literature about cancer rates in babies that weren't breastfed, suggesting that not breastfeeding would give my baby cancer in later life. As I was doing mixed feeding due to the pain, I became worried my baby would die of cot death, and I became unable to sleep, which eventually led to extreme anxiety and not wanting to go out or socialise with other mums because I didn't want to feed my baby in public due to a) pain and b) bei
